name: lake
desc: A gentle young man in his late twenties: the village lamplighter. Tousled wavy brown hair, soft warm brown eyes, a warm boyish friendly face, a calm kind manner. He wears a mid-thigh-length charcoal dark-grey TAILORED COAT with NO HOOD, worn OPEN down the front with no belt: it has an armhole seam at each shoulder, a SLEEVE enclosing each arm down to a cuff at the wrist, and two separate front panels that hang straight down close against his sides. It ends at a plain flat collar band at the base of the neck — nothing bunched or draped behind his shoulders. A small brass flame-shaped clasp at the throat. The open coat shows a white band-collar shirt and, over it, a fitted SCARLET RED-ORANGE vest (the colour of a lit flame) with cord X-lacing down the front. Brown pants, brown boots. No chest strap, no bag, nothing held in either hand. No part of the garment flares or stands out into empty space.
sheetHint: same face, tousled wavy brown hair, warm boyish late-twenties face, open charcoal tailored coat with NO hood, a sleeve on each arm and two front panels hanging straight and close at his sides, plain flat collar band, brass flame-shaped clasp at the throat, white band-collar shirt and a scarlet red-orange X-laced vest beneath, brown pants, brown boots, no chest strap, hands empty

expressions.happy: a bright open smile, eyes lit up
expressions.worried: brows knit, small anxious frown, eyes glancing aside
expressions.determined: firm set jaw, focused eyes, faint confident smirk
expressions.tender: soft eyes, small warm smile, head fractionally tilted — the look of giving someone their name back
expressions.wry: one brow up, mouth pulled a millimetre sideways — the whole joke, delivered quietly and without moving anything else

_framingRef: public/assets/characters/lake/bust-waist.png is THE CUT-IN REFERENCE, and it is bust.png plus 22% of its width in paper margin on each side — nothing else. gen-cutin-art.mjs prefers that filename over bust.png when it exists (its header: 'built per character when the plain bust defeats the framing prompt'). MEASURED 2026-08-02, and it is the framing law again: this bust's coat fills the plate edge to edge at the bottom, so 11 of 12 rest rolls off it drew a figure running off BOTH frame edges — edge_touch 0.096 to 0.181 against cutin_edge's 0.004 gate, i.e. an arm severed by the frame, while the prompt asked in words for 'a little clear space either side' every single time. Padding the REFERENCE fixed it in one go: 5 of the next 6 rolls came back at edge_touch 0.0000 with edge_noise 0.013-0.071. Rebuild it by pasting bust.png centred on a canvas 1.44x its width and filling the pads with the plate's own per-row border paper (skip rows where the border is cloth rather than warm paper, and carry the last paper row down). THE 'NEVER TEXTUAL' CLAUSE THIS NOTE USED TO CARRY IS RETRACTED, on numbers measured in the 2026-08-02 hood-dropped re-roll — it was the same overgeneralisation as _chainNote (b). ASK WHAT CAUSES THE FAULT. A framing fault caused by the REFERENCE is compositional and prose loses to it: the measurement above stands. A framing fault caused by the POSE is textual and a redline wins outright. Same rest plate, same prompt, same everything, one line of tools/characters/cutins.spec.json changed — the `gesture` field rewritten from a MENU OF HAND MOVES ('a hand turned palm-up, a hand laid flat on his own chest, fingers closing around the flame-pin') into a redline naming those two poses as used up and ordering the hands LOW and inside the frame. Before: 8 of 11 moods gated, weary at edge_touch 0.4571 (it drew a SECOND FIGURE running off the right edge), annoyed/hollow/surprised at bot_cut 0.57-0.70 because raised arms widen the lower-torso reference the straight-cut witness divides by. After: 11 of 11 gated, edge_touch 0.0000 on every one, bot_cut 0.84-1.13. NOTE ALSO, same run: this bust does not touch its own plate edges at all (all 1184 border rows warm paper on both sides), so the fault the pad was built for is not even present on it — the pad was rebuilt anyway, cheaply, and the rest roll off it came back edge_touch 0.0000.

turnaround.extraNote: THE GARMENT IS A TAILORED COAT — NOT A CAPE, AND NO LONGER HOODED. The coat part is a MODELLING requirement (2026-08-02, measured — see _capeVerdict): sleeves are set-in on both arms so the arms bind to the ARM joints. The coat is worn OPEN (user pick) and its two front panels must hang STRAIGHT DOWN close against his sides — an open coat's front panels flank the torso right beside the arms, which is the cape's failure geometry at half scale, and the only thing keeping them binding to the spine is staying within a fold's thickness of the body. If char_intake reports those panels arm-weighted, the fallback is to belt the coat closed (art at turnaround-cape-retired/front-belted-superseded.png). THE HOOD IS GONE by user ruling 2026-08-02 ('happy to drop the hood if it's a blocker') — see _chainNote (b): a hood clause re-summoned the cloak silhouette 2 of 2 in the portrait, and a hood is also a free-hanging sheet behind the shoulders, i.e. the same binding hazard in miniature. Dropping it is cheap here and removes both problems at once.

_capeVerdict: 2026-08-02, tools/char_intake.py on the first Tripo delivery. The swept-back cape FAILED to bind: cape panel A 85.9% arm-weighted, panel B 67.1% arm / 27.7% leg, at 7,714 and 6,789 verts (the largest sheet region on any shipped model is Vesper's collar at 1,610). Cause: an auto-rigger binds each vertex to the NEAREST joint, and the cape hung ~35 cm clear of the body, where nothing near it is the spine — under a stride it scissored with the limbs. The swept-back decision itself was VINDICATED in the same pass (arms separate closed loops at 42-52%, same as Finn; both hands 100% clean), so the fix is narrower than a redesign: keep the pose, keep the hood and the charcoal silhouette, close the garment against the body. All five shipped bodies wear coats and all five bind acceptably. Retired art: public/assets/characters/lake/turnaround-cape-retired/. NOTE, superseding an earlier line in this file: while the cape survived as a garment, the cut-ins deliberately drew it draped FORWARD (dramatic chest-up) while the turnaround swept it back (bindable) — one garment, two drapes, which is legitimate because a portrait never animates. That reasoning DIED with the cape. Lake now owns no cape at all, so a cape in a portrait is a plain continuity error and the cut-ins must be re-rolled to the open coat, not merely recoloured.
_lookNote: Identity ratified 2026-08-02 from public/assets/refs/lake.jpeg (user pick: base candidate 3). OPEN coat + FLAME-SCARLET vest are the user's 2026-08-02 picks: they chose the open-front silhouette on look, and asked for a flame colour in place of the green. Three temperatures were rendered (ember-orange, rust-red, flame-scarlet); the user picked SCARLET. My own recommendation had been ember-orange, on the grounds that it sits inside the golden-hour town palette while scarlet fights it — overruled, and the counter-argument I had recorded for scarlet is the one that matters more here: it reads at the town's 65 px character height, where a muted vest disappears.
_chainNote:
TWO SEPARATE CHAINS, AND CROSSING THEM IS A MISTAKE I MADE AND THE USER CAUGHT (2026-08-02).
  * THE 3D CHAIN: turnaround/front.png -> left/right/back -> Tripo. The A-pose is a 3D INPUT.
  * THE PORTRAIT CHAIN: bust.png -> bust-key.png -> cut-ins. Portraits descend from PORTRAITS.
I derived the bust FROM the A-pose, and it came back as a coloured-pencil rendering of a 3D model: stiff, doll-like, no warmth in the face. The user's words: 'the new bust.png style looks like it is downstream of the model, but we should have done this the other way around... We should have just transformed the clothes on bust-cape-superseded.png'. THE RULE: A GARMENT CHANGE IS A CLOTHING EDIT ON THE EXISTING PORTRAIT — keep the drawing, swap the cloth. Never anchor a portrait on the A-pose or anything derived from it.
Two measured constraints that survive from the same day, both instances of ONE law — THE REFERENCE IMAGE DICTATES SHAPE AND FRAMING, AND PROSE ARGUING WITH IT LOSES:
  (a) CROP. Asking for a 'half-body bust' while passing a full-body A-pose returned a full body; passing a chest-up CROP of that same A-pose returned a bust. Same finding the cut-in pipeline measured independently.
  (b) SILHOUETTE — MY EARLIER CLAIM HERE WAS WRONG, AND THE USER CALLED IT. I had written that prose
    cannot overrule a reference's shape, after failing 5 times to turn the cape into a sleeved coat. Their
    reply: "I think this is simply not true in general, and I think we should argue harder / rewrite the
    prompt." They were right. 5 images is not 5 experiments when all 5 use THE SAME PROMPT ARCHITECTURE;
    it is one experiment run 5 times, and I generalised its failure into a law.
    THE CONTROLLED TEST (2026-08-02, docs/qa/lake/prose/, same single reference that beat me, three
    genuinely different architectures, one roll each):
      A 'describe the evidence, never the category' — never says cape or coat, describes only what a
        viewer would SEE (a tube of cloth per arm, a seam over each shoulder point, a turned cuff).
        DESTROYED the cape outright. Overshot: lost the coat body too, leaving sleeves attached to nothing.
      B 'redline the drawing' — names the MISTAKE ("the artist drew a CLOAK when it should be a TAILORED
        COAT"), then defines BOTH garments BY CONSTRUCTION (armhole seam + sleeve + two open front panels
        vs one continuous sheet), then orders the fix. WON OUTRIGHT: a properly tailored open coat, seams,
        cuffs, panels, vest between them. Better than the two-reference result.
      C 'erase, then dress' — two explicit steps. Hybrid: sleeves appeared, drape survived.
    SO THE RULE IS ABOUT WRITING, NOT ABOUT PROSE'S LIMITS. What failed was naming the target category
    and letting the model interpret it ("it is a coat, not a cape"). What works is: name the error, define
    the categories by their CONSTRUCTION, and command a correction to an existing drawing.
    ONE SHARP CAVEAT, measured in the same round: adding "it keeps the hood" to the winning prompt
    RE-SUMMONED THE CLOAK, twice out of two. A hood clause pulls the whole silhouette back toward a cape.
    If a hooded coat must read at chest-up crop, expect to fight that specific clause, or let the hood
    live in the 3D model and other views.
    SHIPPED IN THE END (this paragraph used to say the opposite, and it went stale within the hour): the
    line here was that architecture B stayed an experiment because swapping the bust would orphan a
    freshly gated cut-in suite. Then the user dropped the hood, which removed the only thing B lost, and
    B's bust became public/assets/characters/lake/bust.png (commit 8103203). The 12 cut-ins were re-rolled
    off it the same day and gated 12/12, so nothing was orphaned. The finding and the artifact are both
    live.
  (c) STYLE. Rolls conditioned on a bust drifted to semi-photoreal ~7-head adults 4 times in 5; rolls chained off an already-on-model image held style AND identity 6 of 6. gen-character.mjs's TEXT-ONLY first link was bypassed on purpose — regenerating this face from prose returns a plausible stranger.
